#### Model Validation {#sec-pmc-624}

[**Residuals**]{#sec-pmc-624-residuals}

After fitting the model, we should check whether the model is appropriate.

As with standard [non-linear least squares fitting](#sec-pmd-142), the primary tool for model diagnostic checking is residual analysis.

```{r}
#| label: setup-pmc-624
#| code-fold: true
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

aerosol <- read_table(
  here::here("datasets", "NEGIZ4.DAT"),
  skip = 50,
  col_names = c("Junk1", "Junk2", "ParticleSize", "Junk3", "Junk4")
) |>
  select(ParticleSize)

diff_y <- diff(aerosol$ParticleSize)

fit_ar2 <- arima(diff_y, order = c(2, 0, 0), method = "ML")
fit_ma1 <- arima(diff_y, order = c(0, 0, 1), method = "ML")

resid_ar2 <- as.numeric(residuals(fit_ar2))
resid_ma1 <- as.numeric(residuals(fit_ma1))

four_plot <- function(y) {
  d <- tibble(y = y) |> mutate(order = row_number(), lag_y = lag(y))

  p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(order, y)) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Run Sequence Plot") +
    theme_light()

  p2 <- ggplot(d, aes(lag_y, y)) +
    geom_point(shape = 4) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Lag Plot") +
    theme_light()

  p3 <- ggplot(d, aes(y)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "white", color = "black") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Histogram") +
    theme_light()

  p4 <- ggplot(d, aes(sample = y)) +
    stat_qq() +
    stat_qq_line() +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Normal Probability Plot") +
    theme_light()

  (p1 + p2) / (p3 + p4)
}

acf_plot_single <- function(x, lag_max, title = NULL, xlab = "Lag") {
  n <- length(x)
  a <- acf(x, lag.max = lag_max, plot = FALSE, demean = TRUE)
  r <- as.numeric(a$acf)[-1]
  lag <- as.integer(a$lag)[-1]
  ci95 <- qnorm(0.975) / sqrt(n)

  ggplot() +
    geom_segment(data = tibble(lag = lag, acf = r), aes(lag, y = 0, xend = lag, yend = acf)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = c(ci95, -ci95), color = "steelblue") +
    labs(title = title, x = xlab, y = "Autocorrelation") +
    theme_light()
}
```

[**4-Plot of Residuals from ARIMA(2,1,0) Model**]{#sec-pmc-624-4plot-ar2}

The [4-plot](#sec-eda-4-plot) is a convenient graphical technique for model validation in that it tests the assumptions for the residuals on a single graph.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pmc-624-4plot-ar2
#| fig-cap: "4-plot of residuals from the ARIMA(2,1,0) model"
#| code-fold: true
#| warning: false
four_plot(resid_ar2)
```

[**Interpretation of the 4-Plot**]{#sec-pmc-624-interpretation-4plot-ar2}

We can make the following conclusions based on the above 4-plot.

1. The [run sequence plot](#sec-eda-run-sequence-plot) shows that the residuals do not violate the assumption of constant location and scale. It also shows that most of the residuals are in the range (-1, 1).
2. The [lag plot](#sec-eda-lag-plot) indicates that the residuals are not autocorrelated at lag 1.
3. The [histogram](#sec-eda-histogram) and [normal probability plot](#sec-eda-normal-probability-plot) indicate that the normal distribution provides an adequate fit for this model.

[**Autocorrelation Plot of Residuals from ARIMA(2,1,0) Model**]{#sec-pmc-624-acf-ar2}

In addition, the [autocorrelation plot](#sec-eda-autocorrelation-plot) of the residuals from the ARIMA(2,1,0) model was generated.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pmc-624-acf-ar2
#| fig-cap: "Autocorrelation plot of residuals from the ARIMA(2,1,0) model"
#| code-fold: true
acf_plot_single(resid_ar2, lag_max = 50, title = "Autocorrelation Plot of the Residuals from ARIMA(2,1,0)")
```

[**Interpretation of the Autocorrelation Plot**]{#sec-pmc-624-interpretation-acf-ar2}

The autocorrelation plot shows that for the first 25 lags, all sample autocorrelations except those at lags 7 and 18 fall inside the 95% confidence bounds indicating the residuals appear to be random.

[**Test the Randomness of Residuals From the ARIMA(2,1,0) Model Fit**]{#sec-pmc-624-ljung-ar2}

We apply the [Box-Ljung test](#sec-pmc-4481) to the residuals from the ARIMA(2,1,0) model fit to determine whether residuals are random.

```{r}
#| label: verify-pmc-624-ljung-ar2
#| code-fold: true
ljung_ar2 <- Box.test(resid_ar2, lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 2)
ljung_ar2
```

In this example, the Box-Ljung test shows that the first 24 lag autocorrelations among the residuals are zero ($p$-value = 0.080), indicating that the residuals are random and that the model provides an adequate fit to the data.

[**4-Plot of Residuals from ARIMA(0,1,1) Model**]{#sec-pmc-624-4plot-ma1}

The 4-plot is a convenient graphical technique for model validation in that it tests the assumptions for the residuals on a single graph.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pmc-624-4plot-ma1
#| fig-cap: "4-plot of residuals from the ARIMA(0,1,1) model"
#| code-fold: true
#| warning: false
four_plot(resid_ma1)
```

[**Interpretation of the 4-Plot from the ARIMA(0,1,1) Model**]{#sec-pmc-624-interpretation-4plot-ma1}

We can make the following conclusions based on the above 4-plot.

1. The run sequence plot shows that the residuals do not violate the assumption of constant location and scale. It also shows that most of the residuals are in the range (-1, 1).
2. The lag plot indicates that the residuals are not autocorrelated at lag 1.
3. The histogram and normal probability plot indicate that the normal distribution provides an adequate fit for this model.

This 4-plot of the residuals indicates that the fitted model is adequate for the data.

[**Autocorrelation Plot of Residuals from ARIMA(0,1,1) Model**]{#sec-pmc-624-acf-ma1}

The autocorrelation plot of the residuals from ARIMA(0,1,1) was generated.

```{r}
#| label: fig-pmc-624-acf-ma1
#| fig-cap: "Autocorrelation plot of residuals from the ARIMA(0,1,1) model"
#| code-fold: true
acf_plot_single(resid_ma1, lag_max = 50, title = "Autocorrelation Plot of the Residuals from ARIMA(0,1,1)")
```

[**Interpretation of the Autocorrelation Plot**]{#sec-pmc-624-interpretation-acf-ma1}

Similar to the result for the ARIMA(2,1,0) model, it shows that for the first 25 lags, all sample autocorrelations except those at lags 7 and 18 fall inside the 95% confidence bounds indicating the residuals appear to be random.

[**Test the Randomness of Residuals From the ARIMA(0,1,1) Model Fit**]{#sec-pmc-624-ljung-ma1}

The Box-Ljung test is also applied to the residuals from the ARIMA(0,1,1) model.

```{r}
#| label: verify-pmc-624-ljung-ma1
#| code-fold: true
ljung_ma1 <- Box.test(resid_ma1, lag = 24, type = "Ljung-Box", fitdf = 1)
ljung_ma1
```

The test indicates that there is at least one non-zero autocorrelation among the first 24 lags. We conclude that there is not enough evidence to claim that the residuals are random ($p$-value = 0.026).

[**Summary**]{#sec-pmc-624-summary}

Overall, the ARIMA(0,1,1) is an adequate model. However, the ARIMA(2,1,0) is a little better than the ARIMA(0,1,1).
